lesson_title: Relationships, Tables and Formulae: Finding the Rule in a Bill
hook_text: The plumber charges you before he even opens his toolbox. Here's how to read that bill like a maths teacher.
clip_script: The plumber steps into your yard and you already owe R400. That's the call-out. Then the clock starts: R260 an hour. One hour, R660. Two hours, R920. Three hours, R1 180. Look at the jumps — R260, R260, R260. Same jump every time. That's your rule: something fixed at the start, something extra per unit. Now the flip side. You hire a bakkie for R2 400 and split it. Alone, R2 400. Two of you, R1 200. Three, R800. Six, R400. The bakkie never got cheaper — it just got shared further. Multiply people by price every time and you always land on R2 400. And here's the one that pays you back: the water bill says R699. R160 of that is the basic charge, before a single tap opens. Take it off first — R539 left. Divide by R24,50 a kilolitre — twenty-two kilolitres. Take the fixed part off FIRST, every time. Divide the whole R699 and you'll be out by six and a half kilolitres and a whole mark.
visual_style: A kitchen table stacked with real South African bills — a plumber's invoice, a municipal water statement — the fixed charge circled in one colour and the per-unit rate in another; numbers lifting off the paper into a table and then a straight line.
mood: Calm, streetwise, the voice of someone who has paid these bills.
pacing: Steady through the plumber, quicker through the bakkie split, slow and deliberate on the reverse calculation.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and never guess at a tariff again.
